description: We’re undergraduate and master’s students from Taiwan, combining diverse backgrounds and software development skills. As newcomers to space exploration, we’re excited to learn together and turn NASA’s open data into practical solutions
summary:
Astronauts need to understand their health and respond to problems when immediate medical support is limited. We built Orbital Crew Health to support personal health assessment and coordinated crew assistance.

Each astronaut can check current readings through visual dashboards and trend charts on their phone, comparing them with their personal baseline. Large buttons and focused screens prioritize key information and simple navigation. Three layers work together: NEWS2 scores physiological observations, personal baselines highlight changes over time, and a bilingual AI assistant explains results in plain language, citing the supporting measurements. Core monitoring, records, and first aid resources run locally without a cloud connection.

When someone feels unwell, one request alerts the crew and monitoring station. The monitoring station shows recent health data, while crewmates can open step-by-step first aid cards. Gamified daily exercise and wellbeing tasks combine progress tracking, reminders, and badges to encourage consistent participation.

To demonstrate life on board, we built an explorable 3D spacecraft where users operate crew phones and a shared dashboard connected to the health system. An ESP32 circuit in Wokwi simulates physiological signals. All demonstrations use simulated data.
details:
Orbital Crew Health is an onboard health monitoring prototype designed to help astronauts assess their condition, understand changes over time, and coordinate assistance when immediate medical support is limited. It connects personal crew interfaces, a monitoring station, and a shared dashboard, bringing measurements, personalized analysis, health information, exercise tasks, and emergency notifications into one system.

The system accepts manually recorded measurements and simulated device telemetry. A Python and FastAPI backend validates values, units, timestamps, sources, measurement methods, and quality before storing records in a local SQLite database. Server-Sent Events (SSE) distribute updates to authorized interfaces. Records preserve context such as rest or exercise, posture, and measurement site, allowing subsequent analysis to compare observations collected under similar conditions. Missing, poor-quality, and outdated readings remain visibly distinguishable from usable current data.

Our user interface prioritizes rapid understanding and simple interaction. The phone interface uses large readings, icons, status labels, and trend indicators to help astronauts identify their current state at a glance. Historical charts support different time periods and measurement sources, with access to the records behind individual points. Large buttons lead to focused screens for measurements, training, health trends, the assistant, and first aid. A prominent help button keeps crew assistance accessible. The monitoring station provides a team overview, while the shared dashboard displays selected readings and notifications. This design aims to reduce the effort required to interpret data and locate essential functions during routine work or stressful situations.

We selected complementary health indicators to cover immediate physiological observations, individual changes, and longer-term mission exposure:

  • Heart rate and blood pressure: Microgravity affects fluid distribution and cardiovascular regulation. Tracking heart rate together with systolic and diastolic pressure provides a record of cardiovascular observations, with activity and measurement context retained for comparison.
  • Oxygen saturation and respiratory rate: These provide complementary information about oxygenation and breathing frequency. Their inclusion reflects the importance of respiratory monitoring and oxygen availability in spacecraft environments.
  • Temperature: Temperature trends contribute to physiological assessment. NASA also identifies temperature regulation in microgravity, including potentially faster temperature increases during exercise, as an area requiring further study. We preserve measurement site and method because these affect comparability.
  • Consciousness and supplemental oxygen: These observations complete the context required for NEWS2 scoring, including new confusion and whether supplemental oxygen is being used.
  • Exercise, wellbeing check-ins, and body records: Training participation, self-reported wellbeing, and historical muscle, fat, and injury information add context beyond individual vital-sign readings.
  • Environmental radiation and cumulative exposure: Environmental dose rate describes current conditions, while accumulated exposure preserves a longer-term mission perspective. Radiation information is presented separately from NEWS2.

These choices draw on RCP NEWS2 and NASA research on cardiovascular adaptation, hypoxia, temperature regulation, and space radiation. The team's separate device warning thresholds are prototype testing settings, with their purpose distinguished from the NEWS2 scoring rules.

For health assessment, we implemented a three-layer architecture:

  1. Rule-based assessment and NEWS2 scoring. The first layer implements component scores, a complete total, and score-based bands using the Royal College of Physicians' 2017 NEWS2 scoring charts. It evaluates respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, systolic pressure, heart rate, consciousness, and temperature, together with supplemental oxygen. Diastolic pressure remains available for monitoring and personal analysis but does not contribute to NEWS2. Both oxygen saturation scales are supported; Scale 2 requires explicit confirmation of documented clinical selection.
    The system checks observation completeness, quality, and timing before producing a complete total. When inputs are missing or unusable, available component scores remain visible and the complete total remains unavailable. Each saved assessment preserves its inputs, normalized scoring values, and rule version. Observation grouping and decimal normalization are explicit engineering policies. Separately, a custom sustained resting-heart-rate rule demonstrates automatic crew notifications using synthetic data; NEWS2 scoring itself does not automatically initiate clinical treatment or notifications.
  2. Personal baselines and statistical trends. The second layer compares measurements with the individual's own history. Fixed baselines cover heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, systolic pressure, diastolic pressure, and temperature. Reference samples must match the measurement source, method, and context; resting and exercise observations are analyzed separately. A baseline requires at least 30 eligible observations and nonzero variation.
    A Z-score expresses how far a reading is from the personal mean in standard-deviation units. An exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA), using a weight of 0.2 for new observations, helps reveal persistent changes. This complements NEWS2: in one demonstration, a crew member's heart rate gradually rises from 72 to 84 while the NEWS2 heart-rate component remains zero, but the personal analysis shows the shift from their baseline. Baselines support review, activation, exclusion periods, freezing, and rebuilding. Saved analyses retain the exact baseline and algorithm version used, while gaps and poor-quality data interrupt the analytical sequence appropriately.
  3. Bilingual AI explanations with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The third layer turns saved evidence into understandable English or Traditional Chinese explanations. The backend retrieves the requesting astronaut's authorized measurements, assessments, analyses, and reports. It also searches a local, versioned knowledge library using SQLite FTS5 full-text retrieval and BM25 ranking, selecting relevant bilingual passages with their document and source references.
    The language model receives a bounded set of evidence and must identify the records supporting its answer. The backend checks citation identifiers, numerical consistency, and whether the explanation is supported by the supplied facts. Users can expand citations and ask follow-up questions about the same saved assessment. If the model is unavailable, times out, or fails validation, the interface falls back to local evidence summaries. The assistant explains recorded results and limitations; first-aid procedures are supplied through separately maintained, source-linked cards.

The three layers can be preserved in an assessment report that fixes the NEWS2 version, linked measurements, baseline analyses, alert state, and knowledge versions at the time of saving. Later measurements or baseline changes do not rewrite that report. This makes it possible to revisit the evidence behind an earlier explanation. NEWS2, statistical deviation, and educational information remain separately identifiable rather than being combined into an unsupported overall health score.

When someone feels unwell, a single help request notifies the crew and monitoring station. Monitoring personnel can review recent measurements and assessment summaries, while crewmates can open step-by-step first-aid training cards. These bilingual resources identify their sources, versions, and applicable environments, including microgravity-related training material. Bringing notifications, assessment evidence, and first-aid resources into the same workflow supports coordinated emergency practice.

Gamified daily training connects exercise, measurement, and post-exercise wellbeing tasks. Astronauts can time or manually log exercise, review seven-day progress, receive reminders, and earn badges for accumulated exercise days. Team completion summaries encourage participation while private self-assessment notes remain restricted. An interactive body model complements these routines: users can rotate and select 22 body regions, inspect simulated muscle, fat, and injury records, and compare saved historical snapshots. Radiation views separately show previous exposure and accumulation during the current simulated mission.

To demonstrate the device side, we built an ESP32 telemetry gateway in Wokwi, using two ADS1115 analog-to-digital converters and eight adjustable sliders as simulated sensor inputs. The ESP32 reads the converters over I2C and maps inputs to physiological values. One crew member's readings are controlled through the circuit, while four others use prerecorded synthetic data. ECG heart-rate and posture channels serve as local display inputs; the gateway transmits the supported physiological measurements.

The firmware uses Arduino C++ and FreeRTOS. Separate tasks handle primary vital readings every 0.5 seconds, respiratory updates every two seconds, and network transmission. Mutexes protect shared data, and transmission uses a copied snapshot so that network waits do not hold the measurement-data lock. Device-side logic classifies individual readings using the team's testing thresholds before sending per-crew JSON packets to the backend.

Telemetry packets include UTC timestamps, device and assignment identifiers, sequence numbers, standardized units, activity context, quality, and explicit synthetic-data labels. Paired blood-pressure values share a measurement-group identifier. The gateway handles clock synchronization, Wi-Fi reconnection, and bounded retries; repeated packets retain their identifiers so the backend can recognize them without duplicating records. The documented Wokwi integration demonstrates backend acceptance for all five crew members, including exercise, poor-quality, and missing-data cases. The current demonstration uses HTTP; encrypted transport and persistent buffering remain further deployment work.

We used Three.js and WebGL to create an explorable 3D spacecraft containing living quarters, a shared area, and an exercise zone. Five virtual phones connect to separate crew accounts, and a wall display connects to the shared health dashboard. Users can operate the actual health interface inside the scene, record measurements, request help, and observe updates on the shared display. This provides an interactive demonstration of how the software fits into daily onboard activity and how information reaches people in different parts of the spacecraft.

The software stack combines Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLite, React, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js, with Arduino C++ and FreeRTOS for firmware and Wokwi for circuit simulation. The backend handles model requests, record retrieval, and evidence validation. A reproducible demonstration dataset provides five fictional crew members, 30 days of history, and a five-minute scenario covering stable observations, exercise, gradual deviation, abnormal readings, and data interruption.

Our design considers local availability, personal-data permissions, measurement comparability, interrupted communication, and traceability. Core records, scoring, statistical analysis, first-aid resources, and foreground onboard notifications operate through the local server and network without requiring a cloud model. Detailed personal records and conversations are restricted by role, while shared displays expose selected team information.

The project's creative contribution is the integration of transparent scoring, personal statistics, source-linked AI explanations, engaging health routines, and an interactive spacecraft setting with a working simulated telemetry path. Its intended impact is to strengthen crew autonomy, make health information easier to understand, and support coordinated responses when external assistance is limited. All demonstrations use synthetic data. Physical sensor integration and professional medical validation are future steps toward evaluating real-world reliability and suitability.
